eligibility_reason: MemTX is middleware between an LLM agent and its persistent memory: the agent stages writes ("Staging writes an extracted observation into the transaction as tentative", p.3, §3.1) which pass a validate-and-commit pipeline before becoming action-safe, and later re-enters those records via an explicit read tool scoped to a transaction snapshot (§3.6, p.5: "reading retrieves under the transaction snapshot, staging writes a draft, committing runs the commit pipeline"). The agent's own future tool calls are gated on this stored belief state (§3.3, p.3: irreversible calls are blocked when "some tentative record outside the transaction's snapshot is in flight"), so the store conditions future behaviour across turns/agents. Backbones are LLMs (Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, GLM-4.7-Flash, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.5, p.5), the paper is a 2026 arXiv preprint well over 4 pages (16pp per extraction_note), and text is retrievable. Not E1-E7: the store is written by the agent at run time and is the paper's central contribution, not incidental, not parametric-only, not a fixed corpus, not a survey.

facets.justification: Each record is schema'd with fixed fields — entity, attribute, value, a source with authority weight, a permission block, derived-from edges, a type, a validity interval, and confidence (§3.1, p.3) — and is manipulated through database-style transactional machinery: risk-tiered transactions, five isolation levels, snapshot isolation, and an ordered validate-and-commit pipeline (§3.2, p.3). The paper frames this explicitly as importing "database machinery into agent systems" (p.1) and positions itself against systems built on snapshot isolation, serializable isolation and ChatDB's SQL exposure (p.3). No embedding/similarity, graph-database, or filesystem storage is described for the primary store.

New writes can supersede or correct existing committed records rather than only appending: the semantic-conflict check has "a higher-authority candidate supersedes the old record, a lower-authority one aborts" (§3.2, p.3), and retracting a belief "triggers typed cascading repair of its derived records" (abstract, p.1; §3.1 defines superseded and revoked as lifecycle states, p.3). This is transformation of already-stored content in response to new information, not pure append or synthesis of new higher-level content.

Reads are scoped/filtered by one of five isolation levels defined by which lifecycle states are exposed, from raw-read ("exposing everything") to action-safe-read (§3.1, p.3) — an exact metadata filter on record state, not a ranking. The worked example likewise has an agent read two specific existing records by identity (p.14, Appendix H.4, Turn one: "reads both records"). No embedding similarity, recency decay, or declared multi-method fusion is described.

MemTX is tested on a constructed conformance suite (90 cases, later a 56-case hardened extension) and formally verified by property-based testing and bounded exhaustive enumeration of ~5.5M protocol states (abstract, p.1; §4/Table caption, p.5), compared against 8 baselines across 5 backbones (p.5). No deployment, real users, or fielded system is reported — this is a controlled, in-lab investigation, coded conservatively as validation per the guide's tie-break rule.

The evaluation isolates the memory manager as the sole manipulated variable across otherwise-identical baselines ("so the memory manager is the only variable", p.2), pairs 60 trap cases against 30 controls, and includes ablation variants that graft exactly one MemTX feature onto a baseline lacking it ("Cordon + revocation", "Verified Conc. + gate", "Collaborative + permissions", p.5) to isolate each component's effect.

The contributions list (p.2) states "We design MemTX, a belief-commit state model unifying an eight-state lifecycle, five isolation levels, risk-tiered transactions, action gating on in-flight belief state, and typed cascading repair" — a technique/protocol, which is what the paper argues for; the conformance suite and formal verification are evidence for the method rather than dataset/tool artefacts being the contribution itself.
